newsitem.title: USA: Ferber's defense and prosecutor clash at lunch.
newsitem.headline: Ferber's defense and prosecutor clash at lunch.

text.p: One of the defense lawyers for Mark Ferber, who is waiting to be sentenced after being convicted in August on 58 of 61 counts of fraud and corruption, clashed at a luncheon with one of the former municipal banker's U.S. prosecutors.

The dispute arose over whether or not Ferber, a former executive of Lazard Freres & Co, should have known that he was obliged to fully disclose his fee-splitting arrangement with Merrill Lynch & Co, or whether his case was an effort to make new law.

Kathy Weinman of Dwyer & Collara, who was the featured luncheon speaker at a Bond Buyer conference here on New England public finance, said that from 1990 to 1992 there were no industry standards, rules or regulations defining precisely what should be disclosed.
The charges against Ferber stemmed from his activities during this period. His attorneys have filed a motion for a new trial and a hearing was tentatively set for November 7.

Lazard Freres and Merrill Lynch settled for $24 million a civil case brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which charged the firms had inadequately disclosed their fee-splitting arrangement to issuers. Neither firm admitted or denied the allegations in the settlement.

"Federal prosecutors used broad criminal statutes to prosecute for actions not clearly prohibited by any law, rule or criminal standard. The criminal justice system was used to set standards to punish those who failed to comply when those rules were not in effect," Weinman said.

Her comments prompted David Apfel, an assistant U.S. attorney who helped prosecute the former municipal bond banker, to offer a rebuttal though he said he had promised himself he would not respond to his opponent's speech.

Saying he believed the defense counsel mischaracterised the issue, Apfel said: "Listening to you talk, it's really inconceivable that anyone could have been convicted of the crimes with which Mark Ferber was charged."
In an interview later with Reuters, the prosecutor added that the defendant must have been aware that he had a duty to disclose his relationship to Merrill Lynch.

"I don't know anybody in their right mind who would not think that was wrong when they were in a position to influence the public good," Apfel said. But Apfel saw more room for argument over another issue, whether or not Ferber knew he could be prosecuted as a state employee of Massachusetts under a law barring such workers from accepting gratuities because he worked for a state contractor.
"You could make a straight-faced arguement he did not know he could be construed a state employee," he said.

On this point, Ferber's defense counsel said the state ethics statute had been applied more broadly than ever before, and suggested that in the commercial world, the former municipal bond broker's violation of the gratuity law would have been viewed as marketing.
